plan.topic: Why semaglutide may quiet 'food noise': GLP-1 lowers 'wanting' (dopamine-driven drive) more than 'liking' (pleasure). Wake Forest reward-system research, mostly in animals.
plan.angle: Title: 'Does Semaglutide (Ozempic) Make Food Less Enjoyable? Wanting vs Liking #shorts'. Answer within 10s: in mice, GLP-1 drugs mainly turn down the urge to seek food ('wanting'). The pleasure of eating ('liking') seems less affected. This isn't proven in people yet. Label every finding 'in mice' or 'in people', with a primary source on each. 'Food noise' only as the term people use. Close: eat slowly and stop at comfortably full. Nausea line. Exact prescriber line.
plan.working_title: Does Ozempic Make Food Less Enjoyable? Wanting vs Liking #shorts
plan.why: Wake Forest piece from Oct 5. It copies our #1 GLP-1 Short format (a named-drug mechanism question answered honestly, 'only in animals so far'), and it's a good candidate for the length test. | fact-check: I couldn't verify the 'Wake Forest' attribution. The reward-circuit research I found is mostly in mice: 2026 work showing GLP-1 drugs reduce hedonic feeding via the central amygdala and lower dopamine release (https://www.news-medical.net/news/20260506/GLP-1-weight-loss-drugs-modulate-brain-reward-circuits-to-suppress-eating-for-pleasure.aspx), and animal work where semaglutide reduced cue-driven food seeking while dopamine responses during eating were preserved (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772408523029071). 'Wanting vs liking' is a reasonable reading of that evidence, but it's a hypothesis, not proven in humans. Fixes: (1) Remove 'Wake Forest' unless the scriptwriter cites a specific primary paper from there. (2) Give each finding a source tag plus 'in mice' or 'in people'. (3) The honest answer is 'not proven in humans', not a 'yes'. (4) Mention nausea briefly. The 35-50s length test with a named-drug title is fine.

package.title: Does Semaglutide (Ozempic) Make Food Less Enjoyable? #shorts
package.description:
Scientists split appetite into "wanting" (dopamine drive) and "liking" (pleasure). Animal results on semaglutide are mixed. In a small 12-week trial, 30 adults with obesity, on a lower dose than weight-loss semaglutide, had fewer cravings than placebo — whether it changes enjoyment in humans is unproven. On it? Smaller meals and stopping when full can also ease nausea, a common side effect.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
Brain reward circuit in mice (Nature, 2026): https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10444-4
Semaglutide and dopamine reward signaling (Neuroscience Applied, 2024): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772408523029071
Semaglutide, appetite and food preference in obesity (DOM, 2017): https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.12932
Chronic semaglutide and incentive value of food reward in rats (Psychopharmacology, 2026): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41870532/

social.instagram_caption:
Does a GLP-1 medicine quiet "food noise," or does it dull food's pleasure? The reward science is mostly from mice and rats, and unproven in people 🧠

Researchers split appetite into two circuits:
• Wanting — the dopamine-driven urge to eat
• Liking — the actual pleasure of eating

In mice with human-like GLP-1 receptors, other GLP-1 pills (orforglipron, danuglipron) cut pleasure-eating and dopamine release. But semaglutide's own mouse and rat data are mixed: one mouse study found a single high dose cut sugar rewards collected while dopamine activity during drinking rose. In rats, long-term semaglutide made them work harder for food rewards while eating less overall.

In people, the picture is thinner: a small 12-week trial in 30 adults with obesity (lower dose than weight-loss semaglutide) found fewer cravings than placebo. Whether semaglutide changes "liking" in humans is still unproven.

If you're on it: smaller meals, and stopping when you feel full, can also help ease nausea, a common side effect.

Save this to remember the wanting vs. liking split before your next appointment.

script.hook_pattern: A search-style question about a named drug (semaglutide/Ozempic), answered honestly within about 10 seconds: animal results are mixed and it isn't proven in people. This is the same format as our #1 GLP-1 Short. 'Wanting vs liking' is presented as a framework scientists use, not as a result. With every fact-check fix applied, the script is about 167 spoken words (roughly 78–84s), so it doesn't work as the 35–50s length test. Use a different named-drug Short for that test.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate, honestly hedged and safe. All 7 sources exist, and each one says what the script attributes to it.
- s2: the 2026 Nature paper tested orforglipron and danuglipron in mice with a humanised GLP-1 receptor (Glp1r S33W). The drugs reduced pleasure-driven (hedonic) eating and lowered dopamine signals.
- s3: Kooij et al., Neuroscience Applied vol. 3 (2024). It was in mice and used an acute (one-off) injection. At 1 mg/kg the drug cut the sugar rewards the mice collected, while dopamine-neuron activity in the brain's reward area (VTA) rose as they drank.
- s7: the 2026 Psychopharmacology paper used rats on long-term semaglutide. They pressed harder for a food reward (a progressive-ratio test) but ate less when food was freely available.
- s4: Blundell 2017. A 12-week crossover trial in 30 adults with obesity, funded by Novo Nordisk, found fewer cravings than placebo.
- s1: Berridge & Robinson 2016 is correctly described as a framework, and correctly links 'wanting' to dopamine.

The framing is good:
- The animal results are labelled as animal results.
- The script says the drugs tested in mice are not semaglutide.
- It is clear the wanting/liking split isn't proven in people.
- It includes the side-effect line and the exact prescriber line.

I found 4 minor wording points:
- The advice line should match the cited guidance more closely.
- The s7 on-screen text could contradict the narration when watched with the sound off.
- The s5 dose detail.
- The s7 dose context.

None of these block publishing.

issues.claim: On it? Eat slowly and stop when comfortably full. That can also ease nausea, a common side effect.
issues.problem: The cited guidance (s6, Wharton 2022) recommends smaller meals, stopping once full and avoiding high-fat or spicy foods. I couldn't confirm that it specifically says 'eat slowly'. The advice should match the source it's tagged to.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Some describe this as quieter 'food noise', but trials measure cravings. On it? Try smaller meals and stop when you feel full. That can also ease nausea, a common side effect." Change on_screen_text to: "Smaller meals. Stop when full."

issues.problem: The narration reports a real human finding (fewer cravings vs placebo). The only thing not proven is the wanting/liking split. Someone watching with the sound off could read 'not proven' as 'no effect in people'.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "People: fewer cravings. Wanting vs liking: not proven"

issues.claim: in one mouse study, a single semaglutide dose cut the sugar rewards collected, yet dopamine activity while drinking rose
issues.problem: This is accurate, but only the highest dose tested (1 mg/kg) produced the effect. The lower doses (0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg) didn't change sugar intake or VTA dopamine. Optional precision.
issues.fix: Optional: "Here's the twist: in one mouse study, a single high semaglutide dose cut the sugar rewards collected, yet dopamine activity while drinking rose."

issues.claim: 30 adults with obesity, crossover trial (Novo Nordisk-funded): fewer cravings vs placebo
issues.problem: The trial used semaglutide up to 1.0 mg weekly. That is not the higher dose used for weight management, so viewers may assume it applies to every semaglutide product. Optional context; it's also longer than ideal for a pill.
issues.fix: Optional: "30 adults with obesity, semaglutide 1.0 mg, 12-wk crossover (Novo Nordisk-funded): fewer cravings vs placebo". Keep the text at least ~40px, or shorten to "30 adults, 12 wks, Novo-funded: fewer cravings vs placebo".

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the target window (−13.5 dB under voice) so I trimmed it slightly (0.9×) to keep pauses from creeping above −13 dB. Three swell/tick cues (i32/33 at 18.9s, i73/74 at 54.06s, i93/94 at 70.46s) are mysteriously near-silent (−27 to −32 dB) despite normal gain — likely a rendering glitch on those swells at three key reveal moments (GLP-1 receptors, the 12-week stat, calmer stomach); I pushed them to the 1.5× cap and flagged for regeneration since that alone can't fully restore them. Reduced one spiking swoosh (i35, −4.4 dB) that was briefly louder than the narrator. Thinned two overcrowded flurries (7 near-simultaneous cues each at ~14.2s and ~16.6s, plus one redundant swoosh at 27.8s) down to 3 per moment per the density rule. Added two bespoke accents — a bright discovery chime on the GLP-1-receptor reveal and a soft orchestral sting on the 12-week trial stat — to reinforce those beats given the music dropout there.
